lead: Flash distillation splits a feed into vapour and liquid in one equilibrium stage. The feed is heated, or its pressure dropped, until it partly vaporises. A drum lets vapour leave the top and liquid settle at the bottom. Both products leave in equilibrium. No trays and no reflux: the split is coarse but cheap. Refineries use it before crude distillation, gas plants remove heavy ends, and desalination plants run multi-stage flash.
prereq: You need 4.1 Vapour-liquid equilibrium, Raoult's law and relative volatility for K values and mole fractions.

blocks.text: A flash drum does in one step what a column does in many. It contacts liquid and vapour once, lets them reach equilibrium, and removes them separately. Vapour is richer in the light component; liquid is richer in the heavy component.

items: Feed at F kmol/h and mole fraction z enters a heater.
A valve drops the pressure, taking the feed into the two-phase region.
The mixture enters the drum; vapour disengages and rises, liquid collects at the bottom.
A mist eliminator stops droplets leaving with vapour.
Vapour and liquid leave at drum T and P.
Isothermal flash: heat added so both phases leave at one T.
Adiabatic flash: no heat is added at the drum; the latent heat of the vapour formed comes out of the hot feed's own sensible heat, so the drum runs colder than the feed entering the valve.
Some syllabi call this equilibrium vaporization.

blocks.text: F is feed flow (kmol/h), z its mole fraction, V and L vapour and liquid flows (kmol/h), and y and x their mole fractions. V/F is the vapour fraction: the share of feed leaving as vapour.
F z = V y + L x     and     F = V + L
blocks.where: F feed flow (kmol/h); z feed mole fraction; V, L vapour and liquid flows (kmol/h); y, x their mole fractions.

blocks.text: At equilibrium y<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>i</sub> x<sub>i</sub>. K<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>/x<sub>i</sub> is dimensionless and depends on temperature, pressure and composition. For an ideal mixture K<sub>i</sub> = P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>/P (4.1).

items: Put y = Kx: z = x[(V/F)K + 1 − V/F].

blocks.text: Degrees of freedom decide the drum. Fix T and P: the K values are fixed, so V/F follows — the isothermal flash. Fix the feed enthalpy and the drum pressure instead: no heat is added or removed, and the drum temperature and V/F come out together from the energy balance and Rachford-Rice — the adiabatic flash. At a given P you cannot pin both T and V/F.
The unknown is usually V/F. Both sets of mole fractions must sum to one; combining the sums gives one equation in one unknown.

blocks.where: sum over every component i; z<sub>i</sub> feed mole fraction; K<sub>i</sub> K value at drum T and P; V/F vapour fraction, the unknown.

items: Σ x<sub>i</sub> = 1 gives Σ z<sub>i</sub>/[1 + ψ(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)] = 1, with ψ = V/F.
Σ y<sub>i</sub> = 1 gives Σ z<sub>i</sub> K<sub>i</sub>/[1 + ψ(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)] = 1.
Subtract the first from the second: Σ z<sub>i</sub>(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)/[1 + ψ(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)] = 0.

blocks.text: The left side falls steadily as ψ rises, so when two phases exist there is a single root with 0 < ψ < 1; at the bubble point the root is ψ = 0 and at the dew point ψ = 1. Find the root by trial, bisection or Newton iteration. For two components the equation is linear in ψ, because z<sub>B</sub> = 1 − z<sub>A</sub>:

blocks.where: z<sub>A</sub>, z<sub>B</sub> are feed mole fractions summing to 1; K<sub>A</sub>, K<sub>B</sub> are the two K values at the drum T and P.

blocks.text: Test for two phases first. Both exist only if Σ z<sub>i</sub> K<sub>i</sub> > 1 and Σ z<sub>i</sub>/K<sub>i</sub> > 1. If Σ z<sub>i</sub> K<sub>i</sub> ≤ 1 the feed is below its bubble point and only liquid leaves; if Σ z<sub>i</sub>/K<sub>i</sub> ≤ 1 it is above its dew point and only vapour leaves.

figure.caption: The flash drum of the worked example. The heated feed (F = 100 kmol/h, z<sub>A</sub> = 0.50) drops in pressure across the valve and splits into vapour (y<sub>A</sub> = 0.667) and liquid (x<sub>A</sub> = 0.333), in equilibrium with K<sub>A</sub> = 2.0 and K<sub>B</sub> = 0.5. spec.aria: Flowsheet: feed line through a heater and a valve into a vertical drum with a mist pad near the top; vapour leaves the top at 50 kilomoles per hour with y 0.667 and liquid leaves the bottom at 50 kilomoles per hour with x 0.333.

examples.question: A flash drum receives F = 100 kmol/h of a binary feed with z<sub>A</sub> = 0.50, at a temperature and pressure where K<sub>A</sub> = 2.0 and K<sub>B</sub> = 0.5. Check that two phases form, find V/F from the two-component Rachford-Rice formula, then find V, L, x<sub>A</sub> and y<sub>A</sub>.
steps: Flows: V = 0.50 × 100 = 50 kmol/h and L = 100 − 50 = 50 kmol/h.
Vapour: y<sub>A</sub> = K<sub>A</sub>x<sub>A</sub> = 2.0 × 0.333 = 0.667. For B: x<sub>B</sub> = 0.667 and y<sub>B</sub> = 0.5 × 0.667 = 0.333, so both phases sum to 1.000.
Component balance: V y<sub>A</sub> + L x<sub>A</sub> = 50(0.667) + 50(0.333) = 50.0 kmol/h = F z<sub>A</sub>.
examples.answer: V/F = 0.50, so V = L = 50 kmol/h, with x<sub>A</sub> = 0.333 in the liquid and y<sub>A</sub> = 0.667 in the vapour.
examples.check:
F = 100.0
zA, KA, KB = 0.50, 2.0, 0.5
vf = -(zA*(KA-1) + (1-zA)*(KB-1))/((KA-1)*(KB-1))
V = vf*F
L = F - V
xA = zA/(1 + vf*(KA-1))
yA = KA*xA
print(round(vf,2))
print(round(V,1))
print(round(L,1))
print(round(xA,3))
print(round(yA,3))

traps: Using x = z. The feed composition z is not liquid x; x<sub>i</sub> = z<sub>i</sub>/[1 + (V/F)(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)].
Treating K as constant. K depends on T and P.
Skipping the two-phase test. Solve only when Σ z<sub>i</sub> K<sub>i</sub> > 1 and Σ z<sub>i</sub>/K<sub>i</sub> > 1; otherwise one phase and no root between 0 and 1.
Mixing mass and moles. z, x, y, K and V/F are molar; convert kg/h to kmol/h first.
Confusing flash with simple distillation. In flash vapour stays in contact until equilibrium; in 4.3 vapour is drawn off as it forms.
Taking the vapour fraction as a free choice in an isothermal flash. Once T and P are fixed, V/F follows from Rachford-Rice; to change V/F you change T or P.

quiz.q: Define the K value and state what it depends on.
quiz.a: K<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>/x<sub>i</sub>, the ratio of vapour mole fraction to liquid mole fraction of component i at equilibrium. It depends on temperature, pressure and composition; for an ideal mixture K<sub>i</sub> = P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>/P.

quiz.q: Why does a flash drum give a poorer separation than a distillation column?
quiz.a: It has only one equilibrium stage, so vapour and liquid separate only as much as equilibrium allows at that T and P. A column repeats the contact many times with reflux, so each stage enriches the vapour further.

quiz.q: Distinguish an isothermal flash from an adiabatic flash.
quiz.a: In an isothermal flash heat is supplied so both phases leave at one fixed temperature; T and P are set and V/F follows. In an adiabatic flash no heat is added or removed: the vapour takes its latent heat from the liquid, so the drum temperature falls below the feed temperature, and V/F is fixed by the feed enthalpy at the drum pressure.

quiz.q: A feed of F = 100 kmol/h has z<sub>A</sub> = 0.50, with K<sub>A</sub> = 3.0 and K<sub>B</sub> = 0.5 at the drum condition. Find V/F, V, L, x<sub>A</sub> and y<sub>A</sub>.
For the feed z<sub>A</sub> = 0.50 with K<sub>A</sub> = 2.0 and K<sub>B</sub> = 0.5, find the vapour fraction if the drum were operated at exactly the bubble point of the feed.
quiz.a: At a true bubble point V/F = 0: the liquid is the feed (x<sub>i</sub> = z<sub>i</sub>) and only an infinitesimal bubble of vapour forms, with y<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>i</sub> z<sub>i</sub> and Σ z<sub>i</sub> K<sub>i</sub> = 1. The K values given do not satisfy that: 0.50(2.0) + 0.50(0.5) = 1.25 > 1, so the drum at these conditions is already in the two-phase region and V/F > 0. To reach the bubble point, cool the drum or raise the pressure until Σ z<sub>i</sub> K<sub>i</sub> = 1.

quiz.q: At a proposed drum condition Σ z<sub>i</sub> K<sub>i</sub> works out to 0.85. What happens in the drum and what do you change?
quiz.a: Σ z<sub>i</sub> K<sub>i</sub> = 0.85 < 1 means the drum is below the bubble point of the feed: it stays all liquid, V = 0, no vapour leaves, and there is no Rachford-Rice root between 0 and 1. To flash it, raise the feed temperature or lower the drum pressure so the K values rise until Σ z<sub>i</sub> K<sub>i</sub> > 1 and Σ z<sub>i</sub>/K<sub>i</sub> > 1, then solve Rachford-Rice for V/F.

quiz.q: The drum pressure is raised at constant temperature. Explain the effect on V/F and on the product compositions.
quiz.a: Raising P lowers every K, since K<sub>i</sub> = P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>/P. Lower K means less vapour, so V/F falls. Both products become closer in composition to each other and to the feed: the vapour gets heavier, the liquid gets lighter, and the separation weakens.

beyond: Not for the exam. Multi-stage flash desalination chains drums at falling pressures, each heated by vapour condensing in the next, and supplies drinking water in many coastal cities. Gas processing uses flash calculations for dew-point control and to stabilise condensate before sale. Modern flowsheets compute K values from an equation of state and solve Rachford-Rice inside every unit, so this drum model is the kernel of a process simulator. Search terms: Rachford-Rice, isothermal flash algorithm, PT flash, vapour fraction.
